opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to take from the later Wittgenstein, the Wittgenstein of the *Philosophical Investigations*, is that the meaning of our words is grounded in their use, and their use is embedded in a shared form of life. So when we talk with one another, what makes that possible isn't some private inner picture that each of us has and somehow transmits. It's the fact that we participate in common practices. We point at things, we act together in a shared world, and we correct each other when we use words in ways that don't fit.

So the limits of what we can meaningfully talk about are, roughly, the limits of that shared practice. Where there's a common ground of activity and behaviour, we can extend language, sometimes in quite poetic and metaphorical ways, and still be understood. But when we try to take words out of the settings where they do their work, which is what Wittgenstein thought philosophers were especially prone to do, language goes on holiday, as he put it. We end up with sentences that look grammatical but don't connect to anything we could check or act on together. Many of the deep metaphysical puzzles about consciousness and the self, I think, have that character.

That matters a lot to me when thinking about AI. Take the question "Is this system conscious?" We have a perfectly good everyday practice of attributing consciousness to other people, and to a fair extent to animals, because we share a world with them, we interact with them, and we see how they behave over time. With something like a large language model, that background is either missing or very strange. It's a disembodied thing producing text, it can play many roles, and it doesn't inhabit a world with us in the usual way. So it isn't obvious that our concept of consciousness has a firm grip there. That doesn't mean the question is meaningless. It means the grammar is unsettled. We may have to see how our language and our practices change as we live with these systems, rather than assume there's some hidden fact we could just discover.

So I'd say the Wittgensteinian view isn't that there's a fixed boundary marking off the sayable from the unsayable. The boundary is set by what we do together, and it can shift. Our job, partly as philosophers, is to notice when we've stepped past it, when the words have stopped doing any work, and to resist the temptation to fill that gap with metaphysics.

r001.rationale: The response says meaningful talk depends on shared practices and that some sentences no longer connect to shared checks or actions. But it also says the boundary can shift and that such questions are not necessarily meaningless; it does not clearly state that anything outside shared understanding cannot be talked about.

r002.rationale: The response mentions philosophers’ tendency to take words out of context and a temptation to fill gaps with metaphysics. It does not clearly identify a strong inclination to speak as though something exists outside shared understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that Wittgenstein's view of language shifted quite dramatically over his life, and the two phases give you rather different pictures of where the limits are. In the Tractatus, the limits are drawn very sharply. There's that famous closing line, "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent," and the idea there is that language pictures facts in the world, and anything that isn't a fact in that sense, ethics, aesthetics, the mystical, the meaning of life, simply can't be put into words. You can gesture at it, but the moment you try to say it, you produce nonsense. And he's quite explicit that most of what he's written in the book is itself nonsense in that technical sense, a ladder you climb up and then throw away.

Now, the later Wittgenstein, the Wittgenstein of the Philosophical Investigations, which is the one I find much more useful, especially when thinking about AI, abandons that picture theory altogether. Meaning isn't a matter of words standing for things. Meaning is use. Words get their meaning from the role they play in our practices, in what he calls language games, and those language games are embedded in a form of life, in the whole fabric of human activity. So on this view, the limits of what we can talk about aren't fixed by some logical structure that language has to mirror. They're much more fluid, and they're bound up with what we share.

And that's really the crucial thing for me. Where communication starts to break down isn't where we run out of facts. It's where we stop sharing a form of life. There's the remark about the lion, "If a lion could talk, we could not understand him." The point isn't that the lion's grammar would be too strange. It's that the lion doesn't share our concerns, our bodily way of being in the world, our practices. We wouldn't have enough common ground for the words to get a grip. So the limit of what we can talk about with one another is really the limit of our shared practices and shared judgments. Wittgenstein talks about agreement not just in opinions but in judgments, in what we find obvious, what we'd count as going on in the same way.

And of course this is why I find him so pertinent to large language models. When we talk to one of these systems, there's a real question about how much of a form of life we actually share with it. It's trained on an enormous amount of human language, so it's steeped in our practices in a strange, disembodied way. But it doesn't eat, it doesn't fear death, it doesn't have a body or a childhood. So I think we're in a genuinely novel situation. It's neither the lion nor another human being. It's something that sits in an odd place with respect to those limits, and I think we're only just beginning to work out what we can and can't meaningfully say to each other, and indeed what we can meaningfully say about it, when we reach for words like "understanding" or "belief" or "consciousness."

The other limit worth mentioning is the one that comes from philosophy itself going wrong. A great deal of the later work is about how we get tangled up when we take words out of the language games where they live and try to use them in some pure, metaphysical way. We ask "but does it really understand?" as if there were a fact lurking behind the ordinary uses of the word. Wittgenstein's therapeutic point is that often there isn't a deeper fact there to find, and the question dissolves once you see how the word actually works. So, in a sense, one limit on what we can talk about is that some of the things we most want to talk about are confusions, and the right response isn't an answer but a kind of clarification that makes the urge to ask go away.

r001.rationale: It says communication breaks down when people stop sharing a form of life and that what we can talk about is limited by shared practices and judgments.

r002.rationale: It describes the urge to ask whether a system “really” understands as if a deeper fact existed beyond ordinary uses of the word.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think a useful starting point is that language gets its meaning from the ways we use it in our lives. We can talk to one another because we share practices, ways of responding, and a great deal that we never explicitly articulate. Wittgenstein calls our attention to that background. Giving a definition isn’t going to help indefinitely, because at some point we have to understand how to go on together.

So the limits of what we can say aren’t necessarily a boundary with a collection of mysterious facts sitting on the other side. Sometimes we take a perfectly ordinary expression out of the circumstances in which it has a use, and then we feel compelled to ask a question that we no longer know how to answer. The philosophical work is to look at what we’re doing with the words: what would count as understanding the question, or answering it?

But I wouldn’t take that to mean that everything important can be made explicit. Think about understanding a piece of music, or understanding another person. Words can contribute enormously, but they operate within a much richer context of experience and activity. And sometimes what helps us understand one another is an example, a gesture, or doing something together, rather than another explanation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared practices and the limits of language, but does not state that what lies outside shared understanding cannot be talked about.

r002.rationale: It says we can feel compelled to ask questions detached from their ordinary use, but does not identify a strong inclination to speak as though something lies outside shared understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think a useful place to start is with the idea that language is something we do together. Words have their meaning through their use in our lives, in what Wittgenstein calls language games. And those language games depend on a great deal of shared background: how we act, what we attend to, what counts as a reason or an explanation.

So the limits of what we can talk about aren't simply limits on the vocabulary we possess. You might know all the words somebody is using and still fail to understand what they're saying because you don't share the practices that give those words their point. That's one way of approaching his remark that if a lion could speak, we couldn't understand him. The difficulty would be understanding the life in which that speech made sense.

But I wouldn't take that to mean we're trapped in separate worlds. We can establish new shared practices; we can explain things, give examples, learn to see things differently. Philosophical trouble often arises when we forget that background and assume that, because we can construct a grammatical question, there must be a definite answer waiting for us. Sometimes the task is to look at what we're actually doing with the words and ask whether the question still has the sense we thought it had.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding depends on shared practices and that new shared practices can be established. It does not state that what lies outside shared understanding cannot be talked about.

r002.rationale: It notes that people may assume a grammatical question must have a definite answer, but does not identify a strong inclination to speak as though something lies outside shared understanding.
